Bench: Surya Kant, Dipankar Datta  IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA  CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION  CIVIL APPEAL NO.5827 OF 2023  (Arising out of SLP(Civil) No.2788 of 2021)
 SAVITA KASHYAP APPELLAN  VERSUS  STATE OF U.P. & ORS. RESPONDE  O R D E R 1.
Leave granted.
2. The husband of the appellant was co-sharer in land bearing khasra/plot no.266-C situated in village Ghazipur Saidul Nisha, Pargana & Tehsil Lucknow.

The said land was utilized by State of Uttar Pradesh/Lucknow Development Authority without acquiring the same in accordance with provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (in short 1894 Act) or any other statute.

sentences.text: No award was passed and no compensation was paid to the appellants husband for his share of land.
After approaching the authorities through representation etc., Rakesh Kumar  the husband of the appellant approached the High Court of Judicature Reason: 2014.

The said writ petition was disposed of on 14.05.2019, after taking notice of the fact that pursuant to an order passed by the District Magistrate, the Vice- Chairman, Lucknow Development Authority had deposited a sum of Rs.13,37,991.16 as compensation, out of which 1/6th share had already been withdrawn in the year 2006 by the co-tenure holders/co-sharers (Ravindra Mohan Gupta and Smt. Neelima Gupta).

The High Court further held as follows:-
Since the petitioner was not paid the compensation, he approached to this Court by means of the present writ petition.
After filing of this writ petition, an amount of Rs.11,23,926/- was credited into the account No.30825106698 on 7.9.2015 which is in the name of the petitioner.
In view of the aforesaid, relief No.(i) as claimed in the instant writ petition has been granted by the opposite parties.

2.

In earlier round of litigation, considering the amount of compensation of Rs.11,23,926/- was credited in the bank account number of the petitioner on 9th July,
2015, we, while disposing of the writ petition, granted liberty to the petitioner that if the compensation is inadequate then the petitioner may challenge the same in an appropriate proceedings, in accordance with law.

3. In view of the aforesaid, this writ petition, on the same cause of action, is not maintainable because the petitioner has to challenge the inadequacy of the amount of compensation before the statutory forum, as provided under The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.

sentences.text: 4. The aggrieved appellant is before us.
5. The facts are broadly admitted.
No notification under Sections 4, 6 or any other provision of the 1894 Act was issued in respect of the land owned by deceased husband of the appellant.
No other acquisition process known in law was followed to utilize the said land.

No award was passed and no compensation was paid until the intervention of the High Court, when the District Magistrate wrote a letter to the Lucknow Development Authority and an amount of Rs.13,37,991.16 was deposited,
which included the amount payable to the co-sharers Ravindra Mohan Gupta and Smt. Neelima Gupta.
The deposit of the said amount cannot be termed as an award within the meaning of Section 11 of the 1894 Act.
The action of the authorities in appropriating the land without its lawful acquisition, is thus, patently illegal.

sentences.text: The question which now falls for consideration is as to how the appellant be adequately compensated for the acquired land and how the compensation payable to her be determined?
7. We have heard learned counsel for the parties at a considerable length.
8. The only recourse, in our considered opinion, to be followed for determination of the compensation payable to the appellant is traceable under Section 24(1) of the 2013 Act.
Section 24(1)(a) provides that where no award under Section 11 of the 1894 Act has been made then all the provisions of 2013 Act relating to the determination of compensation shall apply.

We are conscious of the fact that ordinarily clause (a) of sub-section (1) is to be invoked in a case where acquisition process had commenced under the 1894 Act but before any award could be passed under Section 11 thereof,
the old Act was repealed and the 2013 Act came into force.
Here is a case where no acquisition process ever commenced under the 1894 Act and obviously, as noticed earlier, no award under Section 11 of the said Act was passed.
In such a situation, the appellant cannot be left remediless.

The vacuum created due to absence of an express provision to meet with such like situation, can be said to have been adequately addressed by the plain language of clause (a) where it says that when no award under Section 11 of the old Act was passed, then the provisions of the new Act shall apply.

9. In the peculiar facts and circumstances of this case, where the land has been already utilized by the Public Authority, it appears to us that the ends of justice would be adequately met by directing to dispense with the procedure as contemplated under the 2013 Act for acquisition of land, with a further direction to the Collector to determine the market value of the land owned by the appellants husband, as on the date when the 2013 Act came into force i.e., 01.01.2014.

After determining the market value of the land as on 01.01.2014, all other statutory benefits admissible under the 2013 Act including solatium and interest etc., shall also be paid to the appellant minus the amount already paid to the appellant or her husband.
10. The Collector shall pass the award, as directed above, within a period of three months and the compensation amount, so determined, shall be paid to the appellant within four weeks thereafter.
The appellant may accept such compensation amount without prejudice to her right to seek further enhancement of compensation, in accordance with provisions of the 2013 Act.
11. It is clarified that this order shall not ipso facto entitle other co-sharers to revive their claim for enhanced compensation.
12. The appeal stands disposed of in the above terms.
